title: Rules or Learned Patterns?
goals: Execute a stated rule including its boundary
Select a rule by comparing errors on labelled examples
Explain why agreement with fitting examples does not establish performance on new cases
vocabulary: A recorded property used as an input to a decision or model
A recorded category or target associated with an example
A boundary value used in a comparison
Choosing or adjusting a model using examples
The number of predictions that disagree with the comparison labels

blocks.text: Apply threshold 3 to each width before checking the label. Only width 4 disagrees, so its error count is 1. Threshold 5 agrees on all four examples, so its error count is 0. Of these two candidates, this procedure selects 5. Zero disagreements here means it fits these four labels; it is not a guarantee about all future cards.

There can be ties. Threshold 6 also agrees on these four examples because 6 is included by at least. Thresholds 5 and 6 predict differently for width 5, which is absent from the fitting set. The available examples therefore do not uniquely determine how that width should be labelled. A procedure needs an explicit tie rule, and we should record the unresolved case.

guided_practice.title: Complete the supported comparison
guided_practice.prompt: Widths 1, 3, 5, 7 have labels narrow, narrow, wide, wide. For candidates 3 and 5, list all predictions using wide when width is at least the candidate. Count disagreements and select the lower-error candidate.
guided_practice.answer: Threshold 3: narrow, wide, wide, wide; one disagreement at 3. Threshold 5: narrow, narrow, wide, wide; zero disagreements. Select 5 among these candidates based on these examples only.

independent_case.title: Fit a new paper classifier
independent_case.task: A fictional sorting task has lengths 2, 5, 7, 9 cm with labels short, short, long, long. Candidate rules predict long when length is at least 5 or at least 7. List predictions and errors for both, choose one, and predict a new length of 6 before any label is revealed. State one limit of your conclusion.
independent_case.answer: Threshold 5 predicts short, long, long, long: one error at 5. Threshold 7 predicts short, short, long, long: zero errors. Choose 7 and predict short for 6. This fits these supplied labels among these two candidates; the new label, labels at other lengths and general performance are not established.
independent_case.source: primary source W4, first curriculum occurrence

misconceptions: A learned rule cannot be written simply
The selection procedure can fit a single threshold. Complexity is not the definition of fitting.
Zero fitting errors means the model is correct everywhere
Use thresholds 5 and 6, then input 5. Identical fitting scores leave different unseen predictions.
The label is available when predicting
Cover the new case's label until the prediction is recorded. Separate information available at fitting time from prediction time.

CORE IDEA  Fixed instructions and learned behavior can look similar but arise differently.

UNDER THE HOOD  A fixed program's decision logic is specified directly by people. A learned model's parameters are fitted from examples. Both are software, both may be complex, and both can fail; the distinction is how the decision behavior was produced.

blocks.caption: The comparison label is available during fitting and later checking. A new prediction must be made before revealing that case's label.

blocks.text: For threshold t, our rule predicts wide when width is at least t and narrow otherwise. At least includes equality: with t=5, width 5 is wide. Changing at least to greater than changes the rule and may change the error count.

A fitting procedure also contains choices people made: the feature, candidate thresholds, label definition and way of counting errors. Calling a threshold learned does not remove human responsibility for those choices.

blocks.text: CASE 1 — Motion light  Clue: IF motion, THEN light on. Meaning: fixed rule.
CASE 2 — Animal recognizer  Clue: trained on labeled images. Meaning: learned pattern.
CASE 3 — Calculator  Clue: follows arithmetic procedures. Meaning: fixed even when complex.
CASE 4 — Robot vacuum  Clue: behavior alone is incomplete evidence. Meaning: could be fixed, learned, or mixed.
BOUNDARY  Do not use complicated versus simple as a substitute for fixed versus learned.
